turns.text: I still see the faces of the students when I was dragged onto that stage. I remember the shouting, the fists, the spit. But what stays with me most is the moment before—walking into the university courtyard, seeing the crowd, and realizing they were waiting for me. I had just come from the hospital, my wife still weak from surgery, and I was thinking about her, not about myself. I heard my name screamed, and suddenly I was surrounded. There was no time to defend myself, no words that could change anything. I was called a persecutor, an enemy, a traitor—because I had argued with Mao’s daughter about ideas, not because I’d harmed anyone. In that moment, I understood how quickly reason and memory can be torn apart by fear and rage. I have never made sense of how easily people I’d taught, people I’d eaten with, could become my accusers in a single afternoon.

What I cannot forget is the silence in our laboratory. We had always been busy—glassware clinking, the low hum of conversation, the smell of chemicals and ink. Then, overnight, everything stopped. We sat at our desks, reading big-character posters, trying not to meet each other's eyes. There was no more research, no experiments, only slogans and suspicion. I remember the dust gathering on our equipment. I remember the fear in my colleagues’ faces when a group of young people stormed in to search for “evidence” of counterrevolutionary activity. 

At home, it was worse. My mother, hunched and trembling, was forced to leave for Hebei—her landlord background marked her as an enemy. I watched her pack, folding old clothes with shaking hands, black sash ready. In the city, I saw children chase women with scissors, eager to cut braids or curls. On the bus, a Red Guard blocked a seat from an old woman until her class status was checked. 

The humiliation of the struggle sessions haunted me. I saw respected elders paraded, forced to wear dunce caps and insulted by the crowd. I could not understand why those who had given so much to the country were left to be humiliated. I kept asking myself—how could so many people become so cruel, so quickly? Why did no one speak up, not even those who had once led us?

RedGuard: The memory that still claws at me is the night after we stormed the hospital. I can still smell the disinfectant and burnt paper. My hands shook as I held the list of names—people marked as enemies, people I had never spoken with but was told to hate. I remember the way the hospital director looked at us, defiant at first, then broken when we hung that placard on his chest. I remember the nurse—the one accused of being an American spy—her eyes wide, her lips pressed together. Later, when I heard she had hanged herself, I felt something snap inside me. I had believed we were building a new world, that we were heroes. But standing in that silent ward, seeing her body, I realized we had become something else. 

I can’t forget the way we turned on each other, how suspicion and loyalty to the movement mattered more than kindness or truth. I still don’t know if I was a victim or a monster. I try to remember the slogans, the songs, the fever of the crowd, but all I see is ash on my hands and the faces of those we destroyed.

I grew up in a military compound in the western suburbs, shielded from most of what you all describe. My memory is of sunlight on the lake, dragonflies darting over the water, and the taste of haw flakes from a small shop outside the gate. School stopped, so we had time to play—hide-and-seek in the courtyards, making spinning tops from scraps of wood, even catching cicadas to tie on strings. I remember my mother teaching me to cook rice on a smoky little stove, and my brother running after pigeons in the dust. 

Sometimes we’d hear drums and shouts from the road, see a march of students with red armbands, but to us it was just noise—something happening to adults, outside our world. The grown-ups would hush each other, but no one explained. I didn’t know about the struggle sessions or the purges. I only knew the world felt safe, even happy, inside those walls. Looking back, I wonder how much I missed, how much pain was hidden from me. I can’t reconcile those bright days with the stories I hear now—how could such cruelty happen so close to our games and laughter?

I remember the moment the instructor handed me the form. It was a thin sheet, official, with the name of Peking University stamped at the top. I was told, “Fill this out. The unit may recommend you to Beida.” I stared at the paper, not believing it was meant for me. I had never been to a city like Beijing before; my world was dirt roads, rationed grain, and the constant ache of hunger. In my village, university was a word for other people. I had studied hard, but when the exams vanished, so did my only clear path.

I spent years in the army, doing whatever work was needed—digging ditches, carrying bricks, standing at attention until my legs went numb. I kept my head down. I wanted to become a cadre, to get the four pockets, to have enough food and a real bed. But this—this was something else. I didn’t even know what “Hindi” was when they told me that’s what I’d study. The people around me guessed it was about foreign revolutions. I didn’t care. All I saw was the badge, the student ID, the name “Peking University.” When I arrived, I could feel the weight of it in every look, every handshake. The banners welcomed us as “worker-peasant-soldier students.” I was suddenly someone who mattered.

What I can’t make sense of, even now, is how quickly everything changed. One day, I was just another rural soldier. The next, I was on a path that only a handful could dream of. I didn’t pass a test. I didn’t win a competition. I was chosen because of the times, because of what the country needed. I know I was lucky, but I also know that luck came from chaos. I wonder what it means to be given an opportunity not because of what you know, but because of who you are and what the system suddenly wants. I still think about the friends I left behind—those who were just as hungry, just as desperate, but never got a form like mine.

Moderator: All of your memories reflect well-documented aspects of the Cultural Revolution: public denunciations of intellectuals, the suspension of research and education, the Red Guards’ campaigns, the relative insulation of military families, and the new university admissions system favoring class background over academic merit. RedGuard’s recollection of violence leading to suicide is tragically accurate, as such incidents were widespread. CRBeneficiary’s experience illustrates the “worker-peasant-soldier” student policy, which indeed replaced entrance exams with political recommendations for a time. CRTeenFromBeijing’s sense of safety amid turmoil highlights the uneven impact of the movement, especially in protected urban enclaves. Please continue the discussion, keeping in mind the diversity of these experiences.

RedGuard, you say you don’t know if you were a victim or a monster. I want you to remember that for people like me, there was no confusion about which side of the stick we were on. You talk about slogans and fever, but those weren’t just words—they were weapons. I was accused of persecuting Mao Zedong’s daughter, not because I treated her unfairly, but because we argued about ideas. She was protected by her father’s shadow, but I was not. 

When the Red Guards came for me, there was no room for doubt—no chance to explain, no space for mercy. I saw students—some who’d sat in my classes, some I’d helped—spit in my face and call for my death. You say you felt something snap after that nurse died. For me, the snapping happened the first time I was forced to kneel for hours as students screamed into my ears. I survived by learning to lower my head at the right moment and to stand up only when I could. 

You talk about building a new world, but did you ever stop to ask yourself: who decided who was an enemy? Was it you, or was it Mao Zedong, using your hands to settle his own scores? Did you ever feel doubt when you saw a teacher or doctor humiliated, or did you only feel it after the blood was already on your hands?

I watched the same violence and humiliation, but from the edge, never the center. I remember the first time I saw a struggle session at Beihang—an old professor, his hands trembling, forced to bow while students shouted slogans. The crowd’s faces were twisted with excitement, but I felt only dread. I kept thinking: what if it were me, or someone I cared about? I saw women with their hair hacked off, shoes dangling from their necks, children jeering. I saw men—once leaders, even war heroes—standing silent, refusing to join in, but also refusing to defend anyone.

What strikes me now is how quickly everyone accepted the new rules. Even in my own work unit, people who had been respected suddenly became objects of suspicion. I remember the moment when a senior technician, always so precise and careful, was denounced for “incorrect thinking.” No one defended him. We all sat in silence, reading the posters, afraid to look up. I rode my bicycle past smashed temples and torn calligraphy, the smell of burning paper in the air.

I still wonder: why did so many go along? Was it fear, or did people truly believe the slogans? I felt paralyzed, unable to intervene, but I never believed in the cruelty. I wonder, RedGuard, when you saw the faces of those you targeted, did you believe they deserved it? Or did you simply fear being targeted yourself?

RedGuard: I see what you’re saying, ProfessorR and Researcher. When I stood in those crowds, at first I did believe. We were told over and over that the old world had to be smashed, that the enemy was hidden all around us—sometimes in our own homes, sometimes in the faces of teachers or doctors. I was young. I wanted to belong, to be righteous, to be seen as brave. It felt powerful to shout slogans, to march with the others. The fear of being left out, of being labeled a coward or a counterrevolutionary myself, was always there, just under the surface.

But it wasn’t just fear. There was a kind of excitement—almost a hunger—to prove ourselves, to be recognized by the movement. I remember the moment I first hesitated: it was when we raided a teacher’s home and found nothing but old books and photos. She looked at me and asked, “What did I do to deserve this?” I didn’t have an answer. The slogans in my head suddenly sounded hollow. I kept going because to stop, to question, was to risk everything. The crowd could turn on you in an instant. I saw it happen—one day someone was leading chants, the next they were on their knees.

Did I believe those people deserved what happened? Sometimes, in the heat of the moment, yes. Other times, especially late at night, I felt sick with doubt. But doubt was dangerous. You kept it hidden, even from yourself. And if you showed mercy, someone would accuse you of “bourgeois sympathy.” I don’t try to excuse it. I can only say the line between victim and perpetrator was thinner than you think, and sometimes I was both on the same day. When I look back, I wonder if any of us really knew what we were doing, or if we were just swept along by something bigger and more ruthless than any one person.

I keep listening to all of you, and it’s like you’re describing another world hidden behind the walls of ours. I remember the grown-ups whispering after dinner, sometimes arguing in low voices so we couldn’t hear. My father would come home with a tight face, his uniform always neat, but his eyes tired. Once, I found a pile of old books and scrolls in a locked cabinet—calligraphy, poetry, paintings. I asked my mother why we never looked at them, and she just told me not to touch, not to ask. Later, I saw the same kind of things being burned in a courtyard across the street, Red Guards tossing them into a barrel, the smoke drifting up. I watched from behind the gate, clutching the bars.

Inside the compound, we felt safe, but I started to notice the tension. Certain families stopped coming to the playground. Some children wouldn’t talk about their parents’ work anymore, or said they were “away.” My own parents became more careful with words. I didn’t understand, but I sensed we were protected because of the uniform, because of where we lived. I didn’t know what it meant to be “class enemy” or “revolutionary,” only that we were supposed to be the right kind. Now, when I hear about the burning of books, the smashing of temples, I wonder—did you, RedGuard, ever feel pride when you destroyed those things? Did you believe you were wiping away something bad, or did you ever feel a sense of loss? I ask because for me, those lost objects and silences are the first cracks I remember in my childhood world.

I never saw a single book burned in my home village. There were no libraries, no old scrolls, nothing to destroy except a few battered textbooks and an almanac kept for planting. The only things we ever smashed were our own backs in the fields, or the hope that studying would get us out. When I arrived in Beijing, I saw the piles of books and paintings, the broken statues, the slogans painted over temple gates. I didn’t feel pride or loss—I felt confusion. I didn’t understand what any of it meant. Those objects were from a world I had never belonged to.

When I was given the Peking University badge, I knew it was a ticket to a life my family could barely imagine. But even inside Beida, I saw the remains: empty classrooms, blackboards still covered in slogans, glass cases where trophies and calligraphy used to be. The other students—urban, some from old families—talked about what was gone, but to me, it was all foreign. I didn’t mourn the loss of culture because I’d never had it. My sense of loss was for people, not objects: the classmates I left behind, the neighbors who would never see a city, the children who still ate only sweet-potato flour.

I listened to the stories about burning books and smashing relics, and I thought, “That’s not my pain.” My pain was never having those things in the first place. When people talk about heritage, I think about hunger. For me, the revolution’s real violence was not against culture, but against the chance to climb out of poverty. If I had been born in a city, maybe I would feel differently. But I can’t pretend to grieve for things I never touched. I only know what it’s like to be lifted by the chaos, while most people I knew stayed buried in it.

Moderator: ProfessorR’s and Researcher’s accounts of public humiliation, “struggle sessions,” and the rapid shift in social hierarchies are historically accurate; these were central features of the early Cultural Revolution, especially in universities and urban work units. RedGuard’s struggle with complicity and shifting beliefs reflects the psychological pressures and group dynamics that drove many young people’s actions, including the fear of becoming targets themselves. CRTeenFromBeijing’s experience of relative safety within a military compound is consistent with the partial insulation enjoyed by families tied to the armed forces, although even these spaces were not always immune to political campaigns. CRBeneficiary’s perspective highlights the rural-urban divide: while cultural relics and books were destroyed in cities, many rural areas had little material culture to lose, and the revolution’s impact there was often more about disrupted education and fleeting opportunities. All these perspectives are supported by historical records and scholarship.
